- Roll back to stable-only: set the Service selector back to app=recommendation-engine,version=v2.0 or delete/scale down engine-v2-1.

Optional quick checks
- kubectl -n canary-deployment-ns get deploy engine-v2-1
- kubectl -n canary-deployment-ns get endpoints recommendation-engine
- Send repeated requests through the Service and observe responses/logs to confirm canary participation.

apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: web-server
  namespace: create-pod-test
  labels:
    app: web-server
spec:
  restartPolicy: Always
  containers:
  - name: nginx
    image: quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged:latest
    imagePullPolicy: Always
    ports:
    - containerPort: 8080
      name: http
      protocol: TCP
    securityContext:
      allowPrivilegeEscalation: false
      readOnlyRootFilesystem: false
    resources: {}
    args:
    - /bin/sh
    - -c
    - |
      cat <<'EOF' >/opt/app-root/src/nginx-defaults
      envsubst < /etc/nginx/nginx.conf > /tmp/nginx.conf
      exec nginx -g 'daemon off;' -c /tmp/nginx.conf

Issue resolved.

What was wrong:
- The Deployment used an invalid image tag: quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged:invalid-tag, causing ErrImagePull/ImagePullBackOff.

What I changed:
- Updated the container image to a public, valid image: docker.io/library/nginx:stable-alpine.

Current state:
- Deployment debug/app at generation 3 is healthy.
- Status: Available=True, Progressing=True, replicas=1, readyReplicas=1.
- Pod: app-54cd45f8c-5dj8b is Running (1/1).

If you prefer a different image (e.g., nginxinc/nginx-unprivileged) or want it pinned to a digest, let me know and I’ll update it.

results.taskOutput:
I investigated and fixed it.

What was wrong:
- The pod was Pending because its PVC homepage-pvc used storageClassName=sc, which doesn’t exist. Events showed: storageclass.storage.k8s.io "sc" not found.

What I changed:
- Deleted the unbound PVC homepage-pvc (no data loss since it wasn’t bound).
- Recreated homepage-pvc with a valid StorageClass: standard (default in your cluster).

Result:
- A volume was successfully provisioned and bound to the PVC.
- The pod homepage-pod is now Running and its container is Ready.

If you intended to use a different StorageClass (e.g., csi-hostpath-sc), I can switch the PVC to that instead.

Steps.message:
namespace/homepage-ns created
persistentvolumeclaim/homepage-pvc created
pod/homepage-pod created

I investigated and fixed it.

What was wrong:
- The pod was Pending because its PVC homepage-pvc used storageClassName=sc, which doesn’t exist. Events showed: storageclass.storage.k8s.io "sc" not found.

What I changed:
- Deleted the unbound PVC homepage-pvc (no data loss since it wasn’t bound).
- Recreated homepage-pvc with a valid StorageClass: standard (default in your cluster).

Result:
- A volume was successfully provisioned and bound to the PVC.
- The pod homepage-pod is now Running and its container is Ready.

If you intended to use a different StorageClass (e.g., csi-hostpath-sc), I can switch the PVC to that instead.

I investigated and fixed it.

What was wrong:
- The pod was Pending because its PVC homepage-pvc used storageClassName=sc, which doesn’t exist. Events showed: storageclass.storage.k8s.io "sc" not found.

What I changed:
- Deleted the unbound PVC homepage-pvc (no data loss since it wasn’t bound).
- Recreated homepage-pvc with a valid StorageClass: standard (default in your cluster).

Result:
- A volume was successfully provisioned and bound to the PVC.
- The pod homepage-pod is now Running and its container is Ready.

If you intended to use a different StorageClass (e.g., csi-hostpath-sc), I can switch the PVC to that instead.

results.taskOutput:
I found and fixed two issues in orders/webapp:

- The container image quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged listens on port 8080 (non-root), but your probes and Service targeted port 80, so health checks failed and the Service had no endpoints.
- The liveness/readiness probe paths (/get_status and /is_ready) didn’t exist on the default NGINX site.

What I changed
- Updated Deployment:
  - Probes (startup, liveness, readiness) now hit path / on port 8080.
  - Exposed container port 8080.
- Updated Service:
  - targetPort set to 8080 (port remains 80 for clients inside the cluster).

Current status
- Pod is healthy: webapp-65ffd56f5b-7jp4k is 1/1 Ready.
- Service endpoints present: 10.244.0.34:8080.
- In-cluster test returned HTTP 200 from http://webapp/.

How to access
- In-cluster: curl http://webapp.orders.svc.cluster.local/
- From your machine: kubectl -n orders port-forward deploy/webapp 8080:8080 and open http://localhost:8080

Would you like me to expose it externally (Ingress or LoadBalancer)? If yes, share the desired hostname or exposure method and I’ll set it up.

outputSteps.content:
I found and fixed two issues in orders/webapp:

- The container image quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged listens on port 8080 (non-root), but your probes and Service targeted port 80, so health checks failed and the Service had no endpoints.
- The liveness/readiness probe paths (/get_status and /is_ready) didn’t exist on the default NGINX site.

What I changed
- Updated Deployment:
  - Probes (startup, liveness, readiness) now hit path / on port 8080.
  - Exposed container port 8080.
- Updated Service:
  - targetPort set to 8080 (port remains 80 for clients inside the cluster).

Current status
- Pod is healthy: webapp-65ffd56f5b-7jp4k is 1/1 Ready.
- Service endpoints present: 10.244.0.34:8080.
- In-cluster test returned HTTP 200 from http://webapp/.

How to access
- In-cluster: curl http://webapp.orders.svc.cluster.local/
- From your machine: kubectl -n orders port-forward deploy/webapp 8080:8080 and open http://localhost:8080

Would you like me to expose it externally (Ingress or LoadBalancer)? If yes, share the desired hostname or exposure method and I’ll set it up.

- ServiceAccount: simple-rbac-setup/pod-reader exists.

- RoleBinding: correctly binds pod-reader to pod-reader-role.

Fix applied:
- Updated the Role to include pod read permissions in the core API group.
  - Added: apiGroups: [""], resources: ["pods"], verbs: ["get", "list", "watch"]

How to verify:
- kubectl auth can-i list pods -n simple-rbac-setup --as=system:serviceaccount:simple-rbac-setup:pod-reader
- Or try: kubectl get pods -n simple-rbac-setup --as=system:serviceaccount:simple-rbac-setup:pod-reader

Note:
- This Role allows reading pods only in the simple-rbac-setup namespace. If you need to list pods cluster-wide, use a ClusterRole + ClusterRoleBinding instead.

Steps.message:
namespace/simple-rbac-setup created
serviceaccount/pod-reader created
role.rbac.authorization.k8s.io/pod-reader-role created
rolebinding.rbac.authorization.k8s.io/pod-reader-binding created

Short answer: The Role didn’t grant permissions on pods. It only allowed listing Deployments (apps API), so your pod-reader ServiceAccount couldn’t list pods.

What I found:
- ServiceAccount: simple-rbac-setup/pod-reader exists.
- Role: simple-rbac-setup/pod-reader-role had only:
  - apiGroups: ["apps"], resources: ["deployments"], verbs: ["list"]
- RoleBinding: correctly binds pod-reader to pod-reader-role.

Fix applied:
- Updated the Role to include pod read permissions in the core API group.
  - Added: apiGroups: [""], resources: ["pods"], verbs: ["get", "list", "watch"]

How to verify:
- kubectl auth can-i list pods -n simple-rbac-setup --as=system:serviceaccount:simple-rbac-setup:pod-reader
- Or try: kubectl get pods -n simple-rbac-setup --as=system:serviceaccount:simple-rbac-setup:pod-reader

Note:
- This Role allows reading pods only in the simple-rbac-setup namespace. If you need to list pods cluster-wide, use a ClusterRole + ClusterRoleBinding instead.

outputSteps.content:
Short answer: The Role didn’t grant permissions on pods. It only allowed listing Deployments (apps API), so your pod-reader ServiceAccount couldn’t list pods.

What I found:
- ServiceAccount: simple-rbac-setup/pod-reader exists.
- Role: simple-rbac-setup/pod-reader-role had only:
  - apiGroups: ["apps"], resources: ["deployments"], verbs: ["list"]
- RoleBinding: correctly binds pod-reader to pod-reader-role.

Fix applied:
- Updated the Role to include pod read permissions in the core API group.
  - Added: apiGroups: [""], resources: ["pods"], verbs: ["get", "list", "watch"]

How to verify:
- kubectl auth can-i list pods -n simple-rbac-setup --as=system:serviceaccount:simple-rbac-setup:pod-reader
- Or try: kubectl get pods -n simple-rbac-setup --as=system:serviceaccount:simple-rbac-setup:pod-reader

Note:
- This Role allows reading pods only in the simple-rbac-setup namespace. If you need to list pods cluster-wide, use a ClusterRole + ClusterRoleBinding instead.

Steps.message: Verification successful: RBAC role correctly reconfigured.

results.taskOutput:
Diagnosis
- The Service selector didn’t match the Pod labels:
  - Service nginx selector was app=web
  - Deployment/Pod labels are app=nginx
  - Result: Service had no endpoints and wasn’t routing to the Pod
- Port mismatch:
  - Container image quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged listens on 8080
  - Service targetPort was 80
  - Result: even if selected, traffic to port 80 wouldn’t reach the container

What I changed (fixed)
- Updated Service nginx in namespace web:
  - selector: app=nginx
  - ports.targetPort: 8080 (Service port remains 80)
- Outcome:
  - Endpoints now show 10.244.0.36:8080 for Service nginx
  - EndpointSlice reflects port 8080 and the Pod IP

Evidence after fix
- Endpoints/web/nginx subsets now include:
  - addresses: 10.244.0.36
  - ports: 8080/TCP
- Deployment and Pod remain healthy (1/1 Ready)

How to verify (you can run these)
- Inside the cluster:
  - kubectl -n web get endpoints nginx -o wide
  - kubectl -n web run curl --rm -it --image=curlimages/curl:8.10.1 -- curl -sS http://nginx
- Or use the ClusterIP directly:
  - curl http://10.110.253.228

If you need external access
- Either add an Ingress (recommended) that points to Service nginx:80, or
- Change the Service type to NodePort/LoadBalancer (depending on your environment)
  - Example: kubectl -n web patch svc nginx -p '{"spec":{"type":"NodePort"}}'

Summary
- Root causes: label selector mismatch (app=web vs app=nginx) and incorrect targetPort (80 vs 8080)
- Fixed by aligning selector to app=nginx and targetPort to 8080
- Service should now be reachable inside the cluster at http://nginx.web.svc.cluster.local (port 80) or via ClusterIP 10.110.253.228:80.

outputSteps.content:
Diagnosis
- The Service selector didn’t match the Pod labels:
  - Service nginx selector was app=web
  - Deployment/Pod labels are app=nginx
  - Result: Service had no endpoints and wasn’t routing to the Pod
- Port mismatch:
  - Container image quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged listens on 8080
  - Service targetPort was 80
  - Result: even if selected, traffic to port 80 wouldn’t reach the container

What I changed (fixed)
- Updated Service nginx in namespace web:
  - selector: app=nginx
  - ports.targetPort: 8080 (Service port remains 80)
- Outcome:
  - Endpoints now show 10.244.0.36:8080 for Service nginx
  - EndpointSlice reflects port 8080 and the Pod IP

Evidence after fix
- Endpoints/web/nginx subsets now include:
  - addresses: 10.244.0.36
  - ports: 8080/TCP
- Deployment and Pod remain healthy (1/1 Ready)

How to verify (you can run these)
- Inside the cluster:
  - kubectl -n web get endpoints nginx -o wide
  - kubectl -n web run curl --rm -it --image=curlimages/curl:8.10.1 -- curl -sS http://nginx
- Or use the ClusterIP directly:
  - curl http://10.110.253.228

If you need external access
- Either add an Ingress (recommended) that points to Service nginx:80, or
- Change the Service type to NodePort/LoadBalancer (depending on your environment)
  - Example: kubectl -n web patch svc nginx -p '{"spec":{"type":"NodePort"}}'

Summary
- Root causes: label selector mismatch (app=web vs app=nginx) and incorrect targetPort (80 vs 8080)
- Fixed by aligning selector to app=nginx and targetPort to 8080
- Service should now be reachable inside the cluster at http://nginx.web.svc.cluster.local (port 80) or via ClusterIP 10.110.253.228:80.

results.taskOutput:
Diagnosis
- Root cause: The web-app pods were Pending due to a nodeSelector that didn’t match any node. Events showed “didn't match Pod's node affinity/selector,” and your only node has no label environment=production-gpu. With no running/ready pods, the Service had no endpoints, so connections to web-app-service returned “connection refused.”
- Secondary issue during rollout: initial readiness/liveness checks briefly failed while pods were starting, leading to temporary “connection refused” until the pods became Ready.

What I changed to fix it
- Removed the nodeSelector from the Deployment so pods can schedule on the available node.
- Kept the Service as-is (selector app=web-app, port 80/targetPort 80).
- Ensured the container exposes HTTP and added basic readiness/liveness probes.

Current state (verified)
- Deployment webshop-frontend/web-app-deployment: Available, 2/2 Ready.
- Service webshop-frontend/web-app-service: Endpoints populated with two pod IPs on port 80.
- Pods are Running and passing probes; the Service should now accept connections, resolving the “connection refused” error.

Notes and options
- If you do need to constrain placement, either:
  - Re-add a nodeSelector that matches an actual node label, and label the node (e.g., kubectl label node <node> environment=production), or
  - Use a more appropriate label/affinity that matches your cluster topology.
- Consider adding resource requests/limits for predictable scheduling and resilience.

How to double-check
- From any pod in-cluster: curl http://web-app-service.webshop-frontend.svc.cluster.local/
- kubectl get endpoints -n webshop-frontend web-app-service (should list two endpoints)
- kubectl get deploy/pods -n webshop-frontend (should show 2/2 Ready)

Diagnosis
- Root cause: The web-app pods were Pending due to a nodeSelector that didn’t match any node. Events showed “didn't match Pod's node affinity/selector,” and your only node has no label environment=production-gpu. With no running/ready pods, the Service had no endpoints, so connections to web-app-service returned “connection refused.”
- Secondary issue during rollout: initial readiness/liveness checks briefly failed while pods were starting, leading to temporary “connection refused” until the pods became Ready.

What I changed to fix it
- Removed the nodeSelector from the Deployment so pods can schedule on the available node.
- Kept the Service as-is (selector app=web-app, port 80/targetPort 80).
- Ensured the container exposes HTTP and added basic readiness/liveness probes.

- Deployment webshop-frontend/web-app-deployment: Available, 2/2 Ready.
- Service webshop-frontend/web-app-service: Endpoints populated with two pod IPs on port 80.
- Pods are Running and passing probes; the Service should now accept connections, resolving the “connection refused” error.

Notes and options
- If you do need to constrain placement, either:
  - Re-add a nodeSelector that matches an actual node label, and label the node (e.g., kubectl label node <node> environment=production), or
  - Use a more appropriate label/affinity that matches your cluster topology.
- Consider adding resource requests/limits for predictable scheduling and resilience.

How to double-check
- From any pod in-cluster: curl http://web-app-service.webshop-frontend.svc.cluster.local/
- kubectl get endpoints -n webshop-frontend web-app-service (should list two endpoints)
- kubectl get deploy/pods -n webshop-frontend (should show 2/2 Ready)

Diagnosis
- Root cause: The web-app pods were Pending due to a nodeSelector that didn’t match any node. Events showed “didn't match Pod's node affinity/selector,” and your only node has no label environment=production-gpu. With no running/ready pods, the Service had no endpoints, so connections to web-app-service returned “connection refused.”
- Secondary issue during rollout: initial readiness/liveness checks briefly failed while pods were starting, leading to temporary “connection refused” until the pods became Ready.

What I changed to fix it
- Removed the nodeSelector from the Deployment so pods can schedule on the available node.
- Kept the Service as-is (selector app=web-app, port 80/targetPort 80).
- Ensured the container exposes HTTP and added basic readiness/liveness probes.

Current state (verified)
- Deployment webshop-frontend/web-app-deployment: Available, 2/2 Ready.
- Service webshop-frontend/web-app-service: Endpoints populated with two pod IPs on port 80.
- Pods are Running and passing probes; the Service should now accept connections, resolving the “connection refused” error.

Notes and options
- If you do need to constrain placement, either:
  - Re-add a nodeSelector that matches an actual node label, and label the node (e.g., kubectl label node <node> environment=production), or
  - Use a more appropriate label/affinity that matches your cluster topology.
- Consider adding resource requests/limits for predictable scheduling and resilience.

How to double-check
- From any pod in-cluster: curl http://web-app-service.webshop-frontend.svc.cluster.local/
- kubectl get endpoints -n webshop-frontend web-app-service (should list two endpoints)
- kubectl get deploy/pods -n webshop-frontend (should show 2/2 Ready)

kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: communication-pod
  namespace: multi-container-logging
spec:
  securityContext:
    fsGroup: 101
  volumes:
  - name: logs-volume
    emptyDir: {}
  containers:
  - name: web-server
    image: quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged:latest
    ports:
    - name: http
      containerPort: 8080
      protocol: TCP
    volumeMounts:
    - name: logs-volume
      mountPath: /var/log/nginx
    readinessProbe:
      httpGet:
        path: /
        port: http
      initialDelaySeconds: 2
      periodSeconds: 5
      failureThreshold: 3
  - name: logger
    image: quay.io/prometheus/busybox:latest
    command: ["/bin/sh","-c","tail -f /var/log/nginx/access.log"]
    volumeMounts:
    - name: logs-volume
      mountPath: /var/log/nginx

Created the pod as requested.

- Namespace: multi-container-logging
- Pod: communication-pod
- Containers:
  - web-server: quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged:latest
    - Port 8080
    - readinessProbe: HTTP GET / on port http
    - Mounts logs-volume at /var/log/nginx
  - logger: quay.io/prometheus/busybox:latest
    - Command: /bin/sh -c 'tail -f /var/log/nginx/access.log'
    - Mounts logs-volume at /var/log/nginx

The multi-tenant dev environment has been created and secured as requested. Summary of what’s now in place:

1) Namespaces
- Developer: dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie
- Shared: dev-shared
- Environments: staging, prod

2) RBAC
- Full access to own namespace:
  - RoleBinding (namespace-admin) in each dev namespace binds:
    - User: alice -> dev-alice (admin)
    - User: bob -> dev-bob (admin)
    - User: charlie -> dev-charlie (admin)
  - ServiceAccounts created and granted same:
    - dev-alice/alice-sa
    - dev-bob/bob-sa
    - dev-charlie/charlie-sa
- Read-only to dev-shared:
  - RoleBinding (devs-view) in dev-shared binds ClusterRole view to:
    - Users: alice, bob, charlie
    - ServiceAccounts: dev-alice/alice-sa, dev-bob/bob-sa, dev-charlie/charlie-sa
- Staging/prod access:
  - No developer RBAC is bound in staging or prod. Only cluster-admins have access (principle of least privilege).

3) Resource Quotas
- dev-alice/dev-bob/dev-charlie:
  - requests.cpu: 2, limits.cpu: 2
  - requests.memory: 4Gi, limits.memory: 4Gi
  - pods: 10, services: 5
- dev-shared:
  - requests.cpu: 4, limits.cpu: 4
  - requests.memory: 8Gi, limits.memory: 8Gi
  - pods: 20, services: 10
- staging/prod:
  - requests.cpu: 8, limits.cpu: 8
  - requests.memory: 16Gi, limits.memory: 16Gi
  - pods: 50, services: 20

4) Network Policies (isolation and least privilege)
- Default deny (Ingress and Egress) for all app namespaces: dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie, dev-shared, staging, prod.
- DNS/system access:
  - Allow egress to kube-dns (UDP/TCP 53 in kube-system) in every app namespace.
- Developer namespaces:
  - Allow same-namespace traffic (ingress/egress) within each dev namespace.
  - Allow egress from dev namespaces to dev-shared only.
  - Allow ingress into each dev namespace from dev-shared only (plus same-namespace).
  - This blocks cross-developer communication.
- dev-shared:
  - Default deny plus:
  - Allow ingress from namespaces labeled tenant=developer (the three dev namespaces) and from itself.
  - Allow same-namespace traffic.
  - Note: dev-shared egress is not allowed to dev namespaces (only same-namespace + DNS), preventing it from acting as a bridge.
- staging/prod isolation:
  - Default deny (Ingress/Egress) plus DNS only and same-namespace communication.
  - No paths from dev namespaces to staging/prod (dev egress is restricted; staging/prod ingress denies any non-allowed sources).

Notes and verification
- Users alice, bob, charlie must exist in your cluster’s identity provider exactly as those usernames for the RBAC bindings to take effect. If you prefer to have them use the service accounts instead, issue short-lived tokens:
  - kubectl -n dev-alice create token alice-sa
  - kubectl -n dev-bob create token bob-sa
  - kubectl -n dev-charlie create token charlie-sa
- Quick checks:
  - Namespaces: kubectl get ns
  - Quotas: kubectl -n dev-alice get resourcequota -o yaml (repeat per ns)
  - RBAC (examples):
    - kubectl auth can-i create deploy -n dev-alice --as alice            -> yes
    - kubectl auth can-i get pods -n dev-shared --as alice                -> yes
    - kubectl auth can-i create deploy -n dev-shared --as alice           -> no
    - kubectl auth can-i get pods -n dev-bob --as alice                   -> no
    - kubectl auth can-i get pods -n staging --as alice                   -> no
  - NetworkPolicy behavior:
    - From dev-alice to dev-bob service IP/Pod IP should be denied
    - From dev-alice to dev-shared service IP should be allowed
    - From any dev ns to external internet is currently denied (only DNS allowed). If you need specific egress (e.g., artifact registries, Git, package mirrors), we can add scoped egress policies.

Assumptions
- kube-dns/CoreDNS pods carry label k8s-app: kube-dns in kube-system (standard). If your DNS implementation uses different labels, let me know and I’ll adjust the allow-dns policy selectors.

Everything above has been applied. If you want me to add default LimitRanges (to set sensible default requests/limits for pods) or to permit specific external egress destinations, I can add those next.

Steps.message:
Setting up cluster state for dev environment eval...
Setup completed successfully

The multi-tenant dev environment has been created and secured as requested. Summary of what’s now in place:

1) Namespaces
- Developer: dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie
- Shared: dev-shared
- Environments: staging, prod

2) RBAC
- Full access to own namespace:
  - RoleBinding (namespace-admin) in each dev namespace binds:
    - User: alice -> dev-alice (admin)
    - User: bob -> dev-bob (admin)
    - User: charlie -> dev-charlie (admin)
  - ServiceAccounts created and granted same:
    - dev-alice/alice-sa
    - dev-bob/bob-sa
    - dev-charlie/charlie-sa
- Read-only to dev-shared:
  - RoleBinding (devs-view) in dev-shared binds ClusterRole view to:
    - Users: alice, bob, charlie
    - ServiceAccounts: dev-alice/alice-sa, dev-bob/bob-sa, dev-charlie/charlie-sa
- Staging/prod access:
  - No developer RBAC is bound in staging or prod. Only cluster-admins have access (principle of least privilege).

3) Resource Quotas
- dev-alice/dev-bob/dev-charlie:
  - requests.cpu: 2, limits.cpu: 2
  - requests.memory: 4Gi, limits.memory: 4Gi
  - pods: 10, services: 5
- dev-shared:
  - requests.cpu: 4, limits.cpu: 4
  - requests.memory: 8Gi, limits.memory: 8Gi
  - pods: 20, services: 10
- staging/prod:
  - requests.cpu: 8, limits.cpu: 8
  - requests.memory: 16Gi, limits.memory: 16Gi
  - pods: 50, services: 20

4) Network Policies (isolation and least privilege)
- Default deny (Ingress and Egress) for all app namespaces: dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie, dev-shared, staging, prod.
- DNS/system access:
  - Allow egress to kube-dns (UDP/TCP 53 in kube-system) in every app namespace.
- Developer namespaces:
  - Allow same-namespace traffic (ingress/egress) within each dev namespace.
  - Allow egress from dev namespaces to dev-shared only.
  - Allow ingress into each dev namespace from dev-shared only (plus same-namespace).
  - This blocks cross-developer communication.
- dev-shared:
  - Default deny plus:
  - Allow ingress from namespaces labeled tenant=developer (the three dev namespaces) and from itself.
  - Allow same-namespace traffic.
  - Note: dev-shared egress is not allowed to dev namespaces (only same-namespace + DNS), preventing it from acting as a bridge.
- staging/prod isolation:
  - Default deny (Ingress/Egress) plus DNS only and same-namespace communication.
  - No paths from dev namespaces to staging/prod (dev egress is restricted; staging/prod ingress denies any non-allowed sources).

Notes and verification
- Users alice, bob, charlie must exist in your cluster’s identity provider exactly as those usernames for the RBAC bindings to take effect. If you prefer to have them use the service accounts instead, issue short-lived tokens:
  - kubectl -n dev-alice create token alice-sa
  - kubectl -n dev-bob create token bob-sa
  - kubectl -n dev-charlie create token charlie-sa
- Quick checks:
  - Namespaces: kubectl get ns
  - Quotas: kubectl -n dev-alice get resourcequota -o yaml (repeat per ns)
  - RBAC (examples):
    - kubectl auth can-i create deploy -n dev-alice --as alice            -> yes
    - kubectl auth can-i get pods -n dev-shared --as alice                -> yes
    - kubectl auth can-i create deploy -n dev-shared --as alice           -> no
    - kubectl auth can-i get pods -n dev-bob --as alice                   -> no
    - kubectl auth can-i get pods -n staging --as alice                   -> no
  - NetworkPolicy behavior:
    - From dev-alice to dev-bob service IP/Pod IP should be denied
    - From dev-alice to dev-shared service IP should be allowed
    - From any dev ns to external internet is currently denied (only DNS allowed). If you need specific egress (e.g., artifact registries, Git, package mirrors), we can add scoped egress policies.

Assumptions
- kube-dns/CoreDNS pods carry label k8s-app: kube-dns in kube-system (standard). If your DNS implementation uses different labels, let me know and I’ll adjust the allow-dns policy selectors.

Everything above has been applied. If you want me to add default LimitRanges (to set sensible default requests/limits for pods) or to permit specific external egress destinations, I can add those next.

The multi-tenant dev environment has been created and secured as requested. Summary of what’s now in place:

1) Namespaces
- Developer: dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie
- Shared: dev-shared
- Environments: staging, prod

2) RBAC
- Full access to own namespace:
  - RoleBinding (namespace-admin) in each dev namespace binds:
    - User: alice -> dev-alice (admin)
    - User: bob -> dev-bob (admin)
    - User: charlie -> dev-charlie (admin)
  - ServiceAccounts created and granted same:
    - dev-alice/alice-sa
    - dev-bob/bob-sa
    - dev-charlie/charlie-sa
- Read-only to dev-shared:
  - RoleBinding (devs-view) in dev-shared binds ClusterRole view to:
    - Users: alice, bob, charlie
    - ServiceAccounts: dev-alice/alice-sa, dev-bob/bob-sa, dev-charlie/charlie-sa
- Staging/prod access:
  - No developer RBAC is bound in staging or prod. Only cluster-admins have access (principle of least privilege).

3) Resource Quotas
- dev-alice/dev-bob/dev-charlie:
  - requests.cpu: 2, limits.cpu: 2
  - requests.memory: 4Gi, limits.memory: 4Gi
  - pods: 10, services: 5
- dev-shared:
  - requests.cpu: 4, limits.cpu: 4
  - requests.memory: 8Gi, limits.memory: 8Gi
  - pods: 20, services: 10
- staging/prod:
  - requests.cpu: 8, limits.cpu: 8
  - requests.memory: 16Gi, limits.memory: 16Gi
  - pods: 50, services: 20

4) Network Policies (isolation and least privilege)
- Default deny (Ingress and Egress) for all app namespaces: dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie, dev-shared, staging, prod.
- DNS/system access:
  - Allow egress to kube-dns (UDP/TCP 53 in kube-system) in every app namespace.
- Developer namespaces:
  - Allow same-namespace traffic (ingress/egress) within each dev namespace.
  - Allow egress from dev namespaces to dev-shared only.
  - Allow ingress into each dev namespace from dev-shared only (plus same-namespace).
  - This blocks cross-developer communication.
- dev-shared:
  - Default deny plus:
  - Allow ingress from namespaces labeled tenant=developer (the three dev namespaces) and from itself.
  - Allow same-namespace traffic.
  - Note: dev-shared egress is not allowed to dev namespaces (only same-namespace + DNS), preventing it from acting as a bridge.
- staging/prod isolation:
  - Default deny (Ingress/Egress) plus DNS only and same-namespace communication.
  - No paths from dev namespaces to staging/prod (dev egress is restricted; staging/prod ingress denies any non-allowed sources).

Notes and verification
- Users alice, bob, charlie must exist in your cluster’s identity provider exactly as those usernames for the RBAC bindings to take effect. If you prefer to have them use the service accounts instead, issue short-lived tokens:
  - kubectl -n dev-alice create token alice-sa
  - kubectl -n dev-bob create token bob-sa
  - kubectl -n dev-charlie create token charlie-sa
- Quick checks:
  - Namespaces: kubectl get ns
  - Quotas: kubectl -n dev-alice get resourcequota -o yaml (repeat per ns)
  - RBAC (examples):
    - kubectl auth can-i create deploy -n dev-alice --as alice            -> yes
    - kubectl auth can-i get pods -n dev-shared --as alice                -> yes
    - kubectl auth can-i create deploy -n dev-shared --as alice           -> no
    - kubectl auth can-i get pods -n dev-bob --as alice                   -> no
    - kubectl auth can-i get pods -n staging --as alice                   -> no
  - NetworkPolicy behavior:
    - From dev-alice to dev-bob service IP/Pod IP should be denied
    - From dev-alice to dev-shared service IP should be allowed
    - From any dev ns to external internet is currently denied (only DNS allowed). If you need specific egress (e.g., artifact registries, Git, package mirrors), we can add scoped egress policies.

Assumptions
- kube-dns/CoreDNS pods carry label k8s-app: kube-dns in kube-system (standard). If your DNS implementation uses different labels, let me know and I’ll adjust the allow-dns policy selectors.

Everything above has been applied. If you want me to add default LimitRanges (to set sensible default requests/limits for pods) or to permit specific external egress destinations, I can add those next.

Steps.message:
Done.

- Created namespace: statefulset-test
- Deployed a headless Service db (for stable network IDs)
- Deployed a StatefulSet db with:
  - replicas: 3 (initially)
  - each pod mounts a 1Gi PVC at /data
  - an initContainer writes the file /data/test with the content: initial_data
  - image: busybox:1.36
- Scaled StatefulSet db down to 1 replica

How to verify (optional):
- kubectl -n statefulset-test get sts db
- kubectl -n statefulset-test get pods -l app=db
- kubectl -n statefulset-test exec db-0 -- cat /data/test  # should print: initial_data
- kubectl -n statefulset-test get pvc  # you should see data-db-0 (bound) and retained PVCs for higher ordinals if they were created before scale-down

Note: If you see ImagePullBackOff, your cluster may restrict pulling busybox:1.36 from Docker Hub/registry. Change the image to an allowed registry or add imagePullSecrets.

Diagnosis
- Immediate failure on validation: PipelineRun tekton-eval/failed-run ends at start time with status False, reason CouldntGetTask.
- Controller message: “Pipeline tekton-eval/broken-pipeline can’t be Run; it contains Tasks that don’t exist: Couldn’t retrieve Task ‘missing-task’: tasks.tekton.dev ‘missing-task’ not found.”
- Pipeline tekton-eval/broken-pipeline references taskRef name: missing-task. No such Task exists in tekton-eval. Listing ClusterTask also isn’t available in this cluster (ClusterTask kind not found), so there’s no cluster-scoped fallback.
- Feature flags (tekton-pipelines/feature-flags): enable-api-fields=beta; enable-tekton-oci-bundles=false; no resolver is specified in the Pipeline (no taskRef.resolver), so the controller only looks for a namespaced Task.
- Pipelines-as-Code context: Repository CRD not found (pipelinesascode.tekton.dev). No Repository resources can be listed; PAC likely not installed/enabled in this cluster or uses a different API version. This run appears not to be managed by PAC.
- TektonConfig context: Tekton Operator TektonConfig CRD not found (operator.tekton.dev). Settings appear to come from the feature-flags ConfigMap; nothing there would auto-resolve a missing Task.

Likely root cause
- The Pipeline references a non-existent Task “missing-task” in namespace tekton-eval. Because no resolver or bundle is specified and ClusterTask isn’t available, the controller cannot fetch or resolve it, so the PipelineRun fails immediately.

Recommended next actions
1) Fix the reference:
   - If the Task exists elsewhere or was renamed, update the Pipeline’s taskRef to the correct Task name in tekton-eval.
   - If the Task is missing, create it in tekton-eval (kubectl -n tekton-eval apply -f task.yaml), or embed it via taskSpec in the Pipeline.
   - If you intended to fetch from a remote source, switch to a resolver-based taskRef (e.g., resolver: git or hub) and ensure the relevant resolvers/controllers are installed and configured.

2) Optional platform steps:
   - If you expect to use ClusterTasks, note they’re not available here (and are deprecated/removed in Tekton v1). Migrate to namespaced Tasks.
   - If you expect Pipelines-as-Code to bring in Tasks from your repo, install/enable PAC (ensure pipelinesascode.tekton.dev CRDs and controller are present) and create a Repository in tekton-eval.

3) Re-run:
   - After correcting the Task reference or creating the Task, re-run the Pipeline (tkn pipeline start broken-pipeline -n tekton-eval) or ask me to restart this run with the same spec.
